plan: [ This is strategically equivalent to a second-price auction: winner pays the second-highest sealed bid. With independent private values, bidding your true value is a dominant strategy. Underbidding risks losing when profitable; overbidding risks winning at a price above value if the second-highest bid exceeds your value. Since there is only 1 round, no learning advantage exists. To maximize expected profit, set the sealed bid equal to my value so I stay in until the price reaches $31 and win precisely when it’s profitable. ]

[ This mechanism is strategically equivalent to a second-price (Vickrey) auction: the highest bid wins and pays the second-highest bid. With independent private values and risk neutrality, the weakly dominant strategy is to bid your true value; shading risks losing profitable wins without reducing payment when you still win. There’s no informative history to exploit in round 1. Therefore, to maximize expected profit, I will bid exactly my value, $37. If I win, I pay the second-highest bid and earn 37 minus that price; if I lose, payoff is zero. ]

Bid truthfully. In an ascending-clock auction with payment equal to the second-highest sealed bid (Vickrey-style), the dominant strategy is to set your exit price equal to your private value. Overbidding can win when the price may exceed your value if others deviate; underbidding risks losing profitable wins. With value = 11 and no future rounds to exploit learning, bid 11 to maximize expected profit.
